claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a derived high-entropy alloy has high saturation magnetization and coercivity no greater than approximately 100 Oe.
Intermediate-temperature annealing followed by rapid quenching can induce secondary-phase precipitation in an initially single-phase fcc FeCoNi matrix.
The secondary phase produced by the treatment may be ordered.
A suitable annealing window exists in near-equiatomic fcc FeCoNi where slight phase separation occurs without complete phase transformation or excessive grain growth.
The treatment will produce a uniform nanoscale dispersion of precipitates in the fcc matrix.
The precipitates will form coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with the fcc matrix.
Nanoscale precipitates act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Domain-wall pinning raises the energy barrier for magnetization reversal and thereby increases coercivity.
A uniform single-phase structure has less domain-wall pinning than the proposed precipitate-containing structure.
Precipitation-producing annealing can increase coercivity relative to a single-phase state.
The treatment may raise coercivity by several hundred Oe relative to the untreated fcc FeCoNi baseline.
The treatment can largely retain the alloy's high saturation magnetization.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on precipitate volume fraction, size, and distribution.
A secondary phase with reduced magnetic moment could reduce net saturation magnetization.
The controlled experiment will compare heat-treated and untreated samples and use TEM, XRD, and VSM or SQUID to measure precipitates, phase constitution, coercivity, and saturation magnetization.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase, exemplified as an increase greater than approximately 100 Oe, will falsify the hypothesis.
An unacceptable reduction in saturation magnetization will falsify the hypothesis.
